concept_name: One roti, many children
why: Before any word of fractions, the child meets the real question: how big is one share when one whole is shared equally, and does it change when more people share it.
anchor: One roti shared equally between two children, and then among more children: how big is each share?
maths_rules: One roti is the whole; every cut makes equal pieces.
First it is shared between two children, then among more children; the pieces are drawn without numbers or labels.
The open question: how big is one share, and which share is bigger. It is never answered or hinted.
video_title: When more children share one roti, what happens to each share?

concept_name: Halves and quarters of a roti
why: The child meets the first two fractional units, one half and one fourth, as equal shares of one roti, and compares them.
anchor: One roti shared between two children, and one roti of the same size shared among four
wrong_answer: one fourth is more, because four is a bigger number than two
payoff_line: One half of a roti is more than one fourth of a roti

final_answer.spoken: each of two children gets one half, each of four children gets one fourth, and one half is more

maths_rules: 1 roti cut into 2 equal pieces: each piece is 1/2 roti
1 roti of the same size cut into 4 equal pieces: each piece is 1/4 roti
2 pieces of 1/4 fill exactly 1 piece of 1/2, so 1/2 = 2 × 1/4 and 1/2 > 1/4
slip: 4 > 2 does not make 1/4 bigger; more sharers means smaller pieces
your turn: 1 roti among 3 children gives 1/3 each; compare 1/3 with 1/2 (1/2 > 1/3); never shown
video_title: Who gets more roti, two sharing or four sharing?

concept_name: Fractional units: more sharers, smaller share
why: The child compares two unit fractions by thinking of them as shares of the same roti, and meets the name fractional unit.
anchor: A school picnic on a beach in Goa, with one roti shared by five children and another by nine
wrong_answer: one ninth is greater, because nine is bigger than five
payoff_line: One fifth is greater than one ninth

final_answer.spoken: one fifth is greater than one ninth

maths_rules: 1 roti cut into 5 equal pieces: each piece is 1/5 roti
1 roti of the same size cut into 9 equal pieces: each piece is 1/9 roti
more sharers of the same whole means a smaller share, so 1/9 < 1/5 and 1/5 > 1/9
a fractional unit is one of the equal parts of one whole, such as 1/5 or 1/9
slip: 9 > 5 does not make 1/9 bigger; more sharers means smaller pieces
your turn: compare 1/7 and 1/10 of a roti (1/7 > 1/10); never shown
video_title: Which share of a roti is greater, one fifth or one ninth?

concept_name: Measuring a chikki piece in quarters
topic: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole
why: The child names a piece of a whole by how many equal copies of it fill the whole, then measures a bigger piece in that unit.
anchor: A chikki bought from a sweet shop in Lonavala, breaking in two on the way home
wrong_answer: each piece is one half
payoff_line: The small piece is one fourth of the chikki

final_answer.value: small piece 1/4 chikki; bigger piece 3/4 chikki
final_answer.spoken: the small piece is one fourth of the chikki and the bigger piece is three fourths

maths_rules: whole chikki: 6 squares across, 4 down, 6 × 4 = 24 equal small squares
small piece: 3 across, 2 down, 3 × 2 = 6 squares
cutting the chikki in half both ways gives 4 equal pieces of 3 by 2 squares, so 4 copies of the small piece fill the whole: small piece = 1/4
bigger L shaped piece: 24 − 6 = 18 squares = 3 small pieces, so 3 × 1/4 = 3/4
check: 1/4 + 3/4 = 4/4 = 1 whole chikki
slip: two pieces does not make each 1/2; the pieces are not equal
your turn: a slab of gur of 10 equal squares, a piece of 2 squares is 1/5 of it; never shown
video_title: A chikki breaks into two pieces. How much is each piece?

concept_name: Naming the fractional unit of a piece
topic: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole
why: The child names a piece as a fractional unit by counting how many equal copies of it make the whole, then checks with the small squares.
anchor: A chikki bought at a village fair near Mysuru, cut into strips to share
wrong_answer: the strip is one eighth
payoff_line: One strip is one third of the chikki

final_answer.spoken: one strip is one third of the chikki

maths_rules: whole chikki: 6 across, 4 down, 6 × 4 = 24 small squares
2 straight up and down cuts split it into 3 equal strips, each 2 across and 4 down
3 equal strips fill the whole, so one strip is 1/3 chikki
check: one strip has 2 × 4 = 8 squares, and 3 × 8 = 24, the whole chikki
slip: 8 squares in the strip does not make it 1/8; 8 strips of 8 squares would need 64 squares, not 24
your turn: a tray of burfi, 5 across and 2 down, cut into 2 equal rows; one row is 1/2 of the tray; never shown
video_title: One strip of a chikki: what fractional unit is it?

concept_name: Folding a strip into halves, quarters and eighths
why: The child meets length measured in a fractional unit: one unit folded into two equal parts gives two lengths of one half unit.
anchor: Meera folds a paper strip one unit long to make a bookmark at her desk in Chennai
wrong_answer: each part is two units long, because there are two parts
payoff_line: Each part is one half of a unit long

final_answer.spoken: each part is one half of a unit long

maths_rules: the strip is 1 unit long
one fold with the ends meeting makes 2 equal parts
1 unit shared into 2 equal parts: each part is 1/2 unit
check: 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 unit, the whole strip
slip: 2 units for each part would make the 2 parts 4 units together, but the strip is 1 unit
your turn: a strip 1 unit long folded into 5 equal parts gives parts of 1/5 unit; never shown
video_title: Fold a one unit strip once: how long is each part?

concept_name: Collecting halves, and reading fractions
why: The child sees one half as a unit that can be added again and again, and writes each count of halves as an addition statement and as a multiple of one half.
anchor: Harpreet serves half rotis, one at a time, at the langar in Amritsar
wrong_answer: five halves is not a fraction, because a fraction is always less than one
payoff_line: One half added three times is three times one half

final_answer.spoken: one half, then two times one half, three times, four times and five times one half

maths_rules: the unit is 1/2 roti
1/2 + 1/2 = 2 × 1/2, which is 1 full roti
1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 × 1/2, which is 2 full rotis
1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 5 × 1/2, which is 2 full rotis and 1/2 roti
slip: Chintu says five halves is not a fraction; 5 × 1/2 is a real amount, more than 1 roti
your turn: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 3 × 1/3, which is 1 full roti; never shown
video_title: How do you write five half rotis as an addition?

concept_name: Halves and thirds on the number line
topic: Marking Fraction Lengths on the Number Line
why: The child carries the folded strip onto the number line: the unit from 0 to 1 cut into two equal gaps makes the length one half.
anchor: Tanvi watches a tailor measure cloth with a long tape at his shop in Jaipur
wrong_answer: the blue line is one unit long, because it ends at the first mark
payoff_line: The blue line is one half of a unit long

final_answer.spoken: the blue line is one half of a unit long

maths_rules: the number line runs from 0 to 2; the distance from 0 to 1 is 1 unit
0 to 1 is divided into 2 equal parts, so each gap is 1/2 unit
the blue line covers 1 gap from 0, so it is 1/2 unit long
check: 2 gaps of 1/2 make 1 unit, the distance from 0 to 1
slip: the first mark is not 1; the mark for 1 is at the end of the second gap
your turn: 0 to 1 in 4 equal parts, a line from 0 to the first mark is 1/4 unit; never shown
video_title: A blue line stops at the first mark: how long is it?

concept_name: Fifths and eighths on the number line
topic: Marking Fraction Lengths on the Number Line
why: The child reads two lengths in fifths by counting gaps from 0, using the labelled marks to check the count.
anchor: Harpreet runs on her school track in Chandigarh, where flags stand at equal steps
wrong_answer: the shorter line is three fifths, because it touches three marks
payoff_line: The shorter blue line is two fifths of a unit long

final_answer.spoken: two fifths and four fifths of a unit

maths_rules: the number line runs from 0 to 2; each unit is divided into 5 equal parts; each gap is 1/5 unit
the marks 1/5 and 3/5 are labelled (given)
the shorter line ends at the 2nd mark: 2 gaps, 2 × 1/5 = 2/5
the longer line ends at the 4th mark: 4 gaps, 4 × 1/5 = 4/5
slip: the shorter line touches 3 marks (0, 1/5 and the 2nd mark) but covers 2 gaps; the 3/5 label is one gap further
your turn: 0 to 1 in 6 equal parts, lines from 0 to the 2nd and 5th marks are 2/6 and 5/6 unit; never shown
video_title: Fifths on the number line: how long are the two blue lines?

concept_name: Fractions bigger than one whole
topic: Fractions Greater than One and Mixed Numbers
why: The child sorts known fractions by where they end on the number line and meets fractions that are more than one unit.
anchor: Tanvi's walk along a village path, where one unit is the distance from the gate to the well
wrong_answer: all of these lengths are less than one
payoff_line: Some fractions are more than one unit, and they are still fractions

final_answer.spoken: the halves, thirds, fifths up to four fifths, eighths and tenths stop before one, and three halves with the fifths from six to nine go past it

maths_rules: number line from 0 to 2, one unit from 0 to 1
a length less than 1 ends before the mark 1; a length more than 1 ends after it
3/2 = 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2; two halves reach 1, the third half goes past it
6/5, 7/5, 8/5, 9/5 end after 1, since 5 fifths reach 1
slip: Chintu says every length is less than one; 3/2 ends after the mark 1, so he is wrong
your turn: 4/7 ends before 1, 9/7 ends after 1; never shown
video_title: Which of your number line lengths go past one whole unit?

concept_name: Mixed numbers, and back to fractions
topic: Fractions Greater than One and Mixed Numbers
why: The child explains, by counting thirds, why a fraction with more units than make a whole is bigger than one.
anchor: Cups of lassi, each one third of a tall glass, poured at a lassi shop in Amritsar
wrong_answer: four thirds is less than one glass
payoff_line: Four thirds is one third more than a whole, so it is more than one

final_answer.spoken: three thirds already make one whole, and one more third takes four thirds past one

maths_rules: each cup holds 1/3 of a glass
4/3 is 4 cups of 1/3: the first 3 fill 1 glass, the 4th goes past it
4/3 is 1/3 more than 1, so 4/3 > 1
slip: Chintu says four thirds is less than one glass; 3/3 already fill the glass, so he is wrong
your turn: 7/6, since 6/6 = 1 and one more 1/6 makes it more than 1; never shown
video_title: Why is four thirds of a glass more than one glass?

concept_name: Equal lengths on the fraction wall
why: The child sees on three equal strips that one half, two fourths and four eighths cover the same length, and meets the name equivalent fractions.
anchor: Three paper strips of the same length cut for a school chart in Amritsar
wrong_answer: two fourths is longer, because two and four are bigger numbers
payoff_line: One half, two fourths and four eighths are all the same length

final_answer.spoken: yes and yes, the three shaded lengths are equal

maths_rules: 3 strips of the same length; strip A folded into 2 equal parts, 1 shaded: 1/2
strip B folded into 4 equal parts, 2 shaded: 2/4
strip C folded into 8 equal parts, 4 shaded: 4/8
2 pieces of 1/4 fit exactly on 1 piece of 1/2, so 2/4 = 1/2
2 pieces of 1/8 fit exactly on 1 piece of 1/4, so 4 pieces of 1/8 cover 2 pieces of 1/4: 4/8 = 2/4
1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8: the shaded parts of all three strips end at the same place, the middle of the strip
slip: Chintu thinks 2/4 is longer because 2 and 4 are bigger numbers; in fact the shaded lengths are equal
your turn: is 3/4 of a strip the same length as 6/8? (yes, each 1/4 is 2 eighths); never shown
video_title: Is one half of a strip as long as two fourths and four eighths?

concept_name: Equal shares give equivalent fractions
why: The child writes one sharing situation three ways: as a division, as an addition of equal shares, and as a multiplication.
anchor: One hot roti at a roadside dhaba near Ludhiana shared by Harpreet and three cousins
wrong_answer: four divided by one, so each child gets four
payoff_line: One roti is four shares of one fourth

final_answer.spoken: each child gets one fourth; one divided by four is one fourth; four fourths make one; four times one fourth is one

maths_rules: 1 roti cut into 4 equal pieces; each piece is 1/4 roti
division fact: 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4 (the roti is divided, the children divide it)
addition fact: 1 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4
multiplication fact: 1 = 4 × 1/4
slip: Chintu divides 4 by 1 and gives each child 4; one roti cannot give anyone 4 rotis
your turn: 1 roti among 5 children; write the division, addition and multiplication facts (1/5 each); never shown
video_title: One roti, four children: which three facts tell the share?

concept_name: The multiply rule for equivalent fractions
why: The child makes several fractions equal to one half by cutting each half into equal slices, and notices that the denominator is twice the numerator.
anchor: A watermelon Mukta's family cuts on a hot afternoon in Nagpur
wrong_answer: add one to the top and to the bottom
payoff_line: Four eighths, five tenths, six twelfths and seven fourteenths all equal one half

final_answer.spoken: four eighths, five tenths, six twelfths and seven fourteenths

maths_rules: already known: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6
each half cut into 4 equal slices: 8 slices in all, 4 in one half: 4/8 = 1/2
each half cut into 5 slices: 10 in all, 5 in one half: 5/10 = 1/2
each half cut into 6 slices: 12 in all, 6 in one half: 6/12 = 1/2
each half cut into 7 slices: 14 in all, 7 in one half: 7/14 = 1/2
pattern: in each fraction equal to 1/2, the denominator is twice the numerator (8 = 2 × 4, 10 = 2 × 5, 12 = 2 × 6, 14 = 2 × 7)
slip: Chintu adds 1 to the top and the bottom of 1/2 and gets 2/3; 2/3 is more than 1/2, not equal to it
your turn: write three fractions equivalent to 1/4 (cut each fourth into the same number of slices, as in 2/8); never shown
video_title: What other fractions name the same amount as one half?

concept_name: Reducing a fraction to lowest terms
why: The child meets lowest terms for the first time: a fraction can be written with smaller numbers whenever its top and bottom share a common factor.
anchor: Twenty coconut saplings in one row in a Kerala village, sixteen of them watered this morning
wrong_answer: eight tenths, and that is the lowest
payoff_line: Sixteen twentieths in lowest terms is four fifths

final_answer.spoken: sixteen twentieths is not in lowest terms, and in lowest terms it is four fifths

maths_rules: 20 saplings in a row, 16 watered: 16/20 of the row is watered
20 saplings make 5 groups of 4; 16 watered saplings fill 4 of those groups
4 divides 16 and 20 (16 = 4 × 4, 20 = 5 × 4), so 4 is a common factor and 16/20 is not in lowest terms
4 and 5 share no common factor except 1, so 4/5 is in lowest terms
slip: Chintu divides by 2 once to get 8/10 (true, 16/20 = 8/10) and calls it lowest terms; 8 and 10 still share the factor 2, so it is not lowest
your turn: 35/56; 35 = 5 × 7 and 56 = 8 × 7, so 35/56 = 5/8; never shown
video_title: Can 16/20 be written with smaller numbers?

concept_name: Comparing shares of chikki
why: The child compares two shares with different units by rewriting one half in eighths, so both shares are counted in the same unit.
anchor: Groundnut chikki from Lonavala shared at a school picnic, one chikki between two children and five chikkis among eight
wrong_answer: The first group gets more, because only two children share there
payoff_line: each child in the second group gets more

final_answer.spoken: one half is four eighths, which is less than five eighths, so each child in the second group gets more

maths_rules: group 1: 1 chikki shared equally by 2 children, each gets 1/2 chikki
group 2: 5 chikkis shared equally by 8 children; each chikki is cut into 8 pieces and each child takes 1 piece from each, so each gets 5/8 chikki
4/8 < 5/8 because both are counted in eighths and 4 eighths is fewer than 5 eighths
so each child in group 2 gets more
slip: Chintu says group 1 gets more because only 2 children share there; he ignores that group 2 shares 5 chikkis, not 1
your turn: 1 chikki between 2 children or 3 chikkis among 8 children; 1/2 = 4/8 and 3/8 < 4/8, so the pair gets more; never shown
video_title: Who gets more chikki: two sharing one, or eight sharing five?

concept_name: Making the fractional units the same
why: The child compares two pairs of shares, one needing a common unit and one already in the same unit, and says why the second is easier.
anchor: A sugarcane juice stall at a village fair near Kolhapur, where groups of children share glasses of juice
wrong_answer: The ten children get more
payoff_line: the group of four children gets more juice

final_answer.value: 1. Group 1 (3/4 > 7/10); 2. Group 2 (5/7 > 4/7); the second pair was easier, same number of children
final_answer.spoken: the four children get more in the first pair, the five glass group gets more in the second pair, and the second pair is easier

maths_rules: pair 1: 3 glasses among 4 children gives 3/4 each; 7 glasses among 10 children gives 7/10 each
15/20 > 14/20, so 3/4 > 7/10 and the 4 children get more
pair 2: 4 glasses among 7 children gives 4/7; 5 glasses among 7 children gives 5/7; same unit, 5 > 4, so 5/7 > 4/7
pair 2 is easier because both groups have 7 children, so no new unit is needed
slip in words: Chintu says the ten children get more because 7 glasses is more than 3 glasses; he ignores that 10 children share them
your turn: 2 glasses among 3 children or 3 glasses among 5 children; 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15, so the 3 children get more; never shown
video_title: Which group gets more sugarcane juice, and which pair is easier?

concept_name: Adding fractions with the same unit
why: The child adds one half and one fourth by seeing the half as two fourths, so both shares count the same unit.
anchor: A tray of peanut chikki that Meena's father makes at home in winter
wrong_answer: together they ate two sixths
payoff_line: Together they ate three fourths of the chikki

final_answer.spoken: three fourths of the chikki

maths_rules: the whole chikki is cut into 4 equal pieces; each piece is 1/4
Meena's 1/2 covers 2 pieces: 1/2 = 2/4 = 1/4 + 1/4
her brother's share is 1 piece of 1/4
slip: Chintu adds tops and bottoms and gets two sixths; two sixths equals one third, and one third is less than one half, Meena's share alone
your turn: 1/2 + 1/8 = 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8; never shown
video_title: How much chikki did Meena and her brother eat together?

concept_name: Brahmagupta's method for adding
why: The child meets fractions with different units and makes the units the same, here twelfths, before counting.
anchor: A steel glass of lassi that Harpreet makes in Amritsar from curd and water
wrong_answer: it makes two sevenths
payoff_line: One fourth and one third make seven twelfths

final_answer.spoken: seven twelfths

maths_rules: fourths and thirds are different units; they cannot be counted together as they are
3 × 4 = 12, and 12 is a multiple of both 4 and 3
slip: Chintu adds tops and bottoms and gets two sevenths; two sevenths is smaller than one third alone, since 2/7 = 6/21 and 1/3 = 7/21
your turn: 1/5 + 1/2 = 2/10 + 5/10 = 7/10; never shown
video_title: How do we add one fourth and one third?

concept_name: Subtracting fractions with the same unit
why: The child sees subtraction of fractions with the same unit as taking away equal pieces, so only the count of pieces changes and the unit stays.
anchor: Tanvi's chikki bar from Lonavala, cut into seven equal pieces, six of them still with her
wrong_answer: take away the tops and take away the bottoms
payoff_line: Six sevenths take away four sevenths leaves two sevenths

final_answer.spoken: two sevenths of the bar is left

maths_rules: 1 chikki bar cut into 7 equal pieces: each piece is 1/7 of the bar
Tanvi has 6/7 of the bar: 6 pieces of 1/7
she gives 4/7 to Joseph: 4 pieces of 1/7
6 − 4 = 2 pieces of 1/7 are left, so 6/7 − 4/7 = 2/7
slip in words: Chintu takes away the tops and the bottoms; 7 − 7 leaves 0 at the bottom, and no bar is cut into 0 pieces
your turn: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6 (one half); never shown
video_title: What is left when you take four sevenths from six sevenths?

concept_name: Brahmagupta's method for subtracting
why: The child sees that fourths and thirds cannot be taken from each other until both are cut into the same unit, twelfths, as in Brahmagupta's method.
anchor: Two glasses of lassi of the same size at a shop in Amritsar, one three fourths full and one two thirds full
wrong_answer: one whole glass
payoff_line: Nine twelfths take away eight twelfths leaves one twelfth

final_answer.spoken: Harpreet has one twelfth of a glass more

maths_rules: both glasses are the same size; one whole glass is one strip of the same length
Harpreet: 3/4 of a glass; Kavya: 2/3 of a glass
each fourth cut into 3 equal parts: 4 × 3 = 12 parts, and 3/4 covers 3 × 3 = 9 parts, so 3/4 = 9/12
each third cut into 4 equal parts: 3 × 4 = 12 parts, and 2/3 covers 2 × 4 = 8 parts, so 2/3 = 8/12
slip in words: Chintu takes away the tops and the bottoms and gets one whole glass, more than the 3/4 he started with
your turn: 1/2 − 1/5 = 5/10 − 2/10 = 3/10; never shown
video_title: How much more is three fourths of a glass than two thirds?

concept_name: Fractions in India's history
topic: A Pinch of History and the Unit Fraction Puzzle
why: The child connects the idea of equal parts of a broken whole to the old Indian names for a fraction, and learns where our way of writing fractions came from.
anchor: An old manuscript page from ancient India with fractions written one number above another
wrong_answer: the line between the numbers was always there
payoff_line: In ancient India, a fraction was called bhinna, which means broken

final_answer.value: bhinna ('broken'); also bhaga or ansha ('part' or 'piece')
final_answer.spoken: bhinna, which means broken

maths_rules: the old Indian way writes the numerator above the denominator with no line, e.g. 1 above 2 for one half
an old manuscript page from around 300 CE shows fractions written this way
Aryabhata (499 CE), Brahmagupta (628 CE), Sridharacharya (c. 750 CE) and Mahaviracharya (c. 850 CE) used this way of writing
Al-Hassar, a Moroccan mathematician of the 12th century, introduced the line between numerator and denominator
the Indian way of writing reached Europe through the Arabs and came into general use there around the 17th century
names: bhinna means broken; bhaga or ansha means part or piece
Brahmagupta described adding and subtracting fractions with a common denominator
slip: Chintu says the line was always there; it was added later by Al-Hassar
your turn: three fourths in the old way is 3 written above 4 with no line; never shown
video_title: What was a fraction called in ancient India?
